title: Enterprise RAG Architecture
summary: Ingestion through grounded generation, and the failure points that actually show up in production.
components: Ingestion service, chunker, embedding model, vector store, reranker, generation model, citation checker.
dataFlow: Document → ingestion → chunk + embed → vector store → query-time retrieve + rerank → grounded generation → citation check → response.
tradeoffs: Reranking improves precision but adds 100-300ms of latency per query; skipping it is viable only when the vector store's raw top-k is already precise enough for the domain.
scalability: Vector store read load scales with query volume, not corpus size, so sharding decisions should be driven by QPS projections, not document count alone.
failurePoints: Silent retrieval failure (the wrong chunk is retrieved but confidently cited) is the most common and hardest-to-detect failure mode — it doesn't throw an error, it just produces a plausible-sounding wrong answer.
costAnalysis: Embedding cost is one-time per document at ingestion; generation cost recurs per query and dominates total spend once query volume exceeds roughly 10x the corpus size.

body.raw:
## The pipeline

Documents are ingested, chunked, and embedded once. At query time, the system retrieves candidate chunks, reranks them, and generates a response grounded in the retrieved context — then checks that the response's citations actually correspond to retrieved content before returning it.

## The failure mode that matters most

Most RAG failures aren't crashes — they're the system confidently answering from the wrong chunk. That's why the citation-check step exists as a distinct stage, not a side effect of generation: it's the one point in the pipeline explicitly designed to catch silent retrieval failure before it reaches a user.
